analysis.one_liner: Funds removal of lead paint hazards from homes and day-care centers, paid for by a tax on lead.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in two House committees for about 18 months, received a single subcommittee hearing, and died when the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Lead paint in older housing is a leading cause of childhood lead poisoning, which can cause permanent learning and health problems. This bill would have created a permanent program of federal grants to states and big cities to find and remove lead paint hazards in homes and day-care centers, limited to low-income households, and paid for by a new federal tax on lead production and imports. The grant money would come from a dedicated trust fund filled by that tax.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and families living in older, lead-painted housing—especially households earning 80 percent or less of their area's median income—plus day-care centers serving young children. Cities and states with large pre-1960 housing stocks would receive formula grants for inspection, abatement, temporary housing for displaced residents, and lead-poisoning counseling.

how_it_helps.text: Creates an entitlement for states, cities of 100,000 or more, and large urban counties to receive formula grants each year for lead hazard work, funded from a dedicated Lead Abatement Trust Fund [S2][S3].

Grant money can pay for inspecting homes and day-care centers, removing or sealing lead paint, disposing of debris, providing temporary housing for occupants during work, training abatement workers, and counseling families on lead poisoning [S2][S3].

Abatement spending is limited to homes occupied by people earning 80 percent or less of area median income, and owners must record a lien keeping the unit available to low-income occupants for a set period after abatement [S3].
The bill requires certified, trained workers, safety monitoring of abatement sites, and, from 1994, a state or local law enforcing federal abatement standards [S3].
Citizens could sue to force the government to carry out the program's mandatory duties, and prevailing parties could recover attorney fees [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Lead smelters and importers of lead and lead products would pay a new excise tax of 75 cents per pound on primary lead and 37 cents per pound on secondary (recycled) lead for ten years; some of that cost would likely be passed on to buyers of lead products such as batteries. State and local governments would also have to cover a rising share of program costs, from 5 percent the first year to 25 percent after four years.

drawbacks.text: The excise tax would raise the cost of producing and importing lead and lead products, and some of that cost would likely be passed to consumers of goods like batteries and solder [S2][S3].
The grant entitlement exists only to the extent of money in the trust fund, and the tax ends after ten years, so the program would face a funding cliff unless Congress extended it [S3].

Cities and states must provide a growing non-federal match—5 percent rising to 25 percent—which could strain local budgets and smaller jurisdictions; entities with allotments of $250,000 or less get nothing [S3].

The bill ties abatement of privately owned homes to a federal lien and a promise to keep units occupied by lower-income tenants, which some owners might refuse, limiting how much old housing gets treated [S3].
Caps of 10 percent for inspections and 5 percent for monitoring mean most money goes to removal work, with relatively little for finding which homes are dangerous in the first place [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health case was strong: lead paint in pre-1960 housing is a well-documented cause of permanent harm to children, and the bill paired a targeted benefit program with a dedicated funding tax rather than adding to general deficits. The main honest costs are that the tax would raise prices slightly for lead-dependent products, the funding would lapse after ten years, and the rising local match plus lien requirements could limit participation. On balance it was a consequential, targeted program whose costs fell mostly on a specific industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, then to three subcommittees, got one hearing in July 1992, and never reached a committee vote or the House floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced July 17, 1991, by Rep. Cardin with Reps. Waxman and Schroeder, and referred jointly to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees [S5].
It was referred to the Health and the Environment and Transportation and Hazardous Materials subcommittees in October 1991, and to the Select Revenue Measures subcommittee in June 1992 [S5].
The only recorded action after that was a single subcommittee hearing on July 1, 1992; no committee vote, no House floor vote, and no Senate action ever occurred [S5].
By mid-1992 the bill had 47 cosponsors, 46 of them Democrats and one Republican [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, lead smelters, lead importers, and manufacturers of lead products never paid the new per-pound tax, and owners of older housing never faced abatement liens—while families in lead-painted homes got no federal abatement help from this bill.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic: 46 of the 47 cosponsors were Democrats, with a single Republican, and no floor vote ever took place to test broader support.

industries.industry: Primary lead smelters and lead importers
industries.note: The bill would tax primary lead at 75 cents per pound, including imported lead and lead products, for ten years. Their interest in the bill ran against the public's, since the tax that funded abatement came out of their sales.
Recycled lead would be taxed at 37 cents per pound, a cost that would likely flow into prices for products like recycled batteries.

A permanent federal grant program for inspection, removal, and cleanup would create sustained demand for certified abatement work and worker training. The bill caps inspection, monitoring, and training spending, but abatement would be the bulk of spending.

Landlords could have lead hazards removed at federal expense, but only by accepting a lien and keeping units occupied by households at or below 80 percent of area median income for a set period. The benefit and the restriction came together.
